beats.narration_text: Someone wondered if Claude decides which contract issues kill a deal. It doesn't — and that's a design choice, not a limit. The skill runs one fixed screening checklist, every time, and flags matches. Here's what's actually happening under the hood.

beats.narration_text: A skill is a folder Claude reads before it works. This one is diligence-issue-extraction — one file, SKILL.md, written in plain English. No hidden code, no compiled logic, nothing to grep for. Claude reads the file, then acts. The file is the program. They optimized for something a lawyer can audit.

beats.narration_text: The pipeline lives in the Steps section. Claude reads each step in order and runs it. Linear — no branching unless a step spells it out. Predictable, not adaptive. That's the trade.

Here's the interesting constraint. Claude reads each document against a closed list — change-of-control clauses, missing consents, expired licenses — and flags matches. Stay inside the list and the report holds its shape every time. Miss the list, and the skill misses the issue. That's what you buy repeatability with.

beats.narration_text: Same documents in, same report out, every time. Which flagged issue actually kills the deal — that call is still yours. The skill isn't a lawyer; it's a screening pass that never gets tired.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Give it a vendor contract you're actually reviewing, and have it run its own diligence pass: build a checklist of the six deal-critical issues, screen the document against each one, and quote the clause behind every flag. Then go deeper — ask which flagged issue would actually kill the deal, not just show up on the report, and why that distinction matters to a diligence lawyer.

llm_exercise.prompt:
I have a vendor contract I'm reviewing before a deal closes. Paste the contract text below. Before I sign or walk away, run your own due-diligence pass on it. First: build a checklist of the six deal-critical issues a diligence lawyer would screen for — change-of-control, IP assignment vs bare license, indemnity caps, missing third-party consents, expired terms or renewal dates, and termination triggers. Then run every item on the contract and tell me: for each check, what's flagged, what's clean, and what's ambiguous. For every flag, quote the exact clause and explain in one sentence why it matters. End with the one follow-up question I should ask counterparty before I sign.

[paste the contract here]
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: ask the model which flagged issue would actually kill the deal — not just decorate the report — and why that distinction is the whole job of a diligence lawyer, not the checklist.
